newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan imported car sales plunge for second month.
newsitem.headline: Japan imported car sales plunge for second month.

text.p: Imported car sales in Japan fell sharply in May for the second month in a row, depressed by April's sales tax increase, and the downtrend is expected to continue for at least another month, an industry body said on Thursday.

The Japan Automobile Importers Association (JAIA) said imported vehicles sold in Japan in May fell 27 percent from a year earlier to 22,919 units. In April, imported car sales slipped nearly 37 percent to 20,869 units.

Consumers continued to keep their distance from big-ticket items like cars following a rise in the national sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1, said Kunihiko Ono, vice-chief secretary of JAIA.
A decrease in the number of cars made abroad by Japanese carmakers and an increase in the price of some foreign car models in April also contributed to the drop, he said.
Sales in Japan of vehicles produced by overseas units of Japanese carmakers totalled 2,517 in May, down 58.3 percent from a year earlier, the association said.

After the rush of purchases ahead of the tax rise subsided, Rover Japan, the Japanese unit of the Rover Group, increased prices on 16 of its 26 models by an average of 5.3 percent, while Ford Motor Co raised the price of its four models by about 2.7 percent. Both increases were made to compensate for the recent weakness of the yen, Ono said.
Rover is the British unit of Bayerische Motoren-Werke AG.
"Foreign automakers held down their prices until the increase in the consumption tax, as the rush of demand allowed them to sell more cars," he said.
Ono said sales of imported cars in Japan would probably fall again in June but after that the pace of the decline should slow, helped by the release of new models.
Saturn Japan, a division of General Motors Corp's GM N Japanese unit, announced on Thursday that it sold 80 cars in May, compared to 60 in April.

"Given that it is less than 60 days since we started sales and that we have a relatively small number of outlets, we are not disappointed in these results," said Keith Wicks, General Director of Saturn Japan.
Ono added, "New models and aggressive marketing could brighten up foreign car sales later this year," but he did not say when he expected sales to start picking up.

Ono said the Tokyo Motor Show, which starts at the end of October, could help loosen Japanese consumers' purse strings, provided the launch of new models, a stable economy and a favourable exchange rate coincide.
In addition, many more car owners than usual are expected to replace their vehicles this year, said Yoshio Watanabe, an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics Inc.
"Japanese people buy new cars every seven years or so, and an immense number of cars were sold seven years ago," he said.
At that time, the Japanese economy was in the final stages of its "bubble" era of inflated asset prices.
